entries.name: Breadth-first beam search
entries.persistent_id: Beam-Stack Search: Integrating Backtracking with Beam Search
entries.definition: A heuristic search procedure that advances by depth layers, retaining at most a chosen beam width of the best-ranked candidate nodes for each next layer and discarding the other candidates.
entries.identity_notes: This record denotes the conventional breadth-first form of beam search. Wider historical uses of beam search also include global best-first frontier truncation and other heuristic pruning procedures. A width of one follows a single surviving continuation; it is not the unbounded global-frontier algorithm curated as greedy best-first search.

source.title: Beam-Stack Search: Integrating Backtracking with Beam Search
source.version: ICAPS 2005 proceedings, 90–98; official conference PDF with unnumbered pages

entries.locator: Background: Beam search, PDF p. 1; breadth-first scope on PDF p. 2
entries.mechanism: Expand the retained nodes in the current depth layer, rank their eligible successors with the chosen heuristic or evaluation rule, and retain at most the beam width for the next layer. Candidates removed by this width rule are not systematically recovered by the basic procedure.
limitations: Width pruning can discard every path to a solution or every optimal path, so basic beam search has no general completeness or optimality guarantee.
A layer-width bound does not by itself bound all memory: stored predecessor information, retained earlier layers, generated successors and any global duplicate table must also be accounted for.

Ranking, ties, goal stopping and duplicate handling are additional choices. Increasing the beam width does not guarantee an improvement in returned solution quality for every implementation and problem.

entries.name: Best-first beam search with a global frontier cap
entries.definition: A best-first search procedure that limits the entire open frontier to a fixed number of nodes by discarding the worst-ranked frontier nodes when that capacity is exceeded.
entries.identity_notes: The qualified name identifies the global frontier truncation described in the 2005 and 2010 search papers. A shared name does not equate those pruning rules.

source.title: A Comparison of Greedy Search Algorithms
source.version: SoCS 1(1), 129–136 (2010); author-hosted manuscript with unnumbered PDF pages

entries.locator: Beam Search, PDF p. 4: best-first versus breadth-first beams
entries.mechanism: Select the best-ranked node from the current open frontier and add its eligible successors. Whenever the frontier exceeds the chosen capacity, discard its worst-ranked nodes until it fits. Candidates from different depths can therefore compete for the same finite frontier slots.
limitations: Global frontier pruning can permanently remove a needed path; the cap alone establishes neither completeness nor optimality.
The cap applies to the open frontier, not automatically to closed tables, predecessor storage, generated successors or the total program memory.
No equivalence to breadth-first beam output, monotonic quality with larger width, or universal runtime advantage is asserted.

entries.name: Beam-stack search
entries.persistent_id: Beam-Stack Search: Integrating Backtracking with Beam Search
entries.definition: A layer-based beam search augmented with a stack of admitted evaluation ranges so that backtracking systematically revisits successors previously discarded by beam-width pruning.
entries.identity_notes: Beam-stack search combines breadth-first beam expansion with chronological backtracking and an incumbent solution-cost bound. It is distinct from permanent beam pruning, limited-discrepancy beam backtracking, and the separately named iterative-deepening BSIDA-star variant.

source.title: Beam-Stack Search: Integrating Backtracking with Beam Search
source.version: ICAPS 2005 proceedings, 90–98; official conference PDF with unnumbered pages

entries.locator: Beam-stack search, PDF pp. 2–3; Theorem 1, PDF pp. 3–4
entries.mechanism: Use an admissible cost estimate f=g+h and an incumbent upper bound U. For each expanded layer, store a range of successor evaluations admitted to the next beam. Width pruning records the smallest rejected evaluation as the upper endpoint. On backtracking, advance the deepest unfinished range and regenerate that layer’s successors. Improved solutions lower U; exhaustion of the stack ends the improvement search.
limitations: The paper’s termination and optimality argument assumes finite branching, a positive lower bound on operator cost and a finite initial upper bound supplied by an actual solution, together with admissible pruning. It is not a guarantee for arbitrary zero-cost cycles, an infinite bound or arbitrary duplicate policies.
Ties require a consistent ordering, or enough beam capacity to retain the unbroken tie group; a bare numeric range with unresolved ties is insufficient.
The baseline retains up to a beam of nodes per depth layer plus the beam stack. O(w*d) node storage does not mean a fixed total-memory cap independent of search depth.

The initially supplied solution must remain available if no improvement is found. An upper-bound number alone is not a returned path; this record does not certify the displayed pseudocode as a complete implementation.

entries.name: Divide-and-conquer beam-stack search
entries.persistent_id: Beam-Stack Search: Integrating Backtracking with Beam Search
entries.definition: A beam-stack search implementation that retains a small set of search layers and relay information, regenerates missing layers for backtracking, and reconstructs a solution through recursive subproblems.
entries.identity_notes: DCBSS is the divide-and-conquer implementation of beam-stack search described by Zhou and Hansen. Unlike divide-and-conquer beam search without backtracking, it retains beam-stack range information that permits previously discarded layers to be regenerated and searched further.

source.title: Beam-Stack Search: Integrating Backtracking with Beam Search
source.version: ICAPS 2005 proceedings, 90–98; official conference PDF with unnumbered pages

entries.locator: Memory efficiency and Divide-and-conquer beam search, PDF p. 4; Divide-and-conquer beam-stack search and Figure 1, PDF p. 5; continuation on PDF p. 6
entries.mechanism: Retain the current, previous, successor and relay layers, with relay references used to divide path reconstruction into smaller searches. If chronological backtracking reaches a layer no longer stored, replay from the start using the saved beam-stack ranges to rebuild it. For the general non-unit-cost case in the paper, retain the best goal information and delay path reconstruction until backtracking begins.
limitations: Four retained node layers do not imply constant total storage: the beam stack still has depth-dependent entries, and path output, temporary successors and reconstruction state also require memory.
Discarding layers trades storage for regeneration and reconstruction work; no universal runtime improvement is implied.

The underlying beam-stack pruning, tie handling and bounded-search assumptions still matter. Layered duplicate detection must be matched to the graph setting; the paper distinguishes directed and undirected behavior.

The paper summarizes recursive solution recovery and refers to earlier work for implementation details. This record supports the described mechanism, not a complete executable reconstruction implementation.

entries.name: Beam search using limited discrepancy backtracking
entries.definition: A memory-bounded beam search that explores heuristic-ranked slices using increasing limited-discrepancy budgets and removes backtracked slices so that alternative beams can be examined.
entries.identity_notes: BULB denotes Furcy and Koenig’s Beam search Using Limited discrepancy Backtracking. A discrepancy selects a nonpreferred successor slice; it is not a numerical heuristic error or an action cost. The inspected algorithm is presented for unit-cost state-space search and seeks a path, not necessarily a shortest path.

source.title: Limited Discrepancy Beam Search
source.version: IJCAI 2005 proceedings; official conference PDF with unnumbered pages

entries.locator: Sections 2–3.3, PDF pp. 2–4; Figure 4 on PDF p. 3
entries.mechanism: Keep one slice of up to the beam width at each active depth. Rank eligible successors by heuristic value and divide them into slices. A probe follows the preferred slice without spending discrepancy allowance and explores nonpreferred slices with a reduced allowance, removing slices from the active hash table on backtracking. Outer iterations increase the allowance; a full table causes the current probe to stop and backtrack.
limitations: Completeness is conditional on enough memory to store a beam along a solution path. A fixed memory budget and arbitrary beam width do not guarantee solving every instance.
The method need not return a shortest path. An anytime extension is discussed separately from the base procedure.
The O(B*d) storage statement concerns retained slices along the active search; temporary successor generation, heuristic data and other implementation storage need separate accounting.
The active hash table prevents cycles involving retained states and some transpositions, but it is not a permanent global closed list of every state ever visited.

Figure 4 has an apparent depth-label inconsistency: nextSlice labels a successor with depth although the caller next probes depth+1. The prose describes a next-level slice. This record follows that described mechanism and does not certify the literal pseudocode as executable.
